title: The Musnad
hookLine: his vast collection of reports, arranged by Companion

lines: TWO WAYS TO SHELVE A LIBRARY.
BY SUBJECT, OR BY WHO TOLD YOU.
cards: There are two ways to shelve a library of sayings. By subject: everything on prayer here, everything on fasting there, trade in the next room.
Or by who told you: every story your grandmother told on one shelf, every story your uncle told on the next. Sahih al-Bukhari, whose opening report was yesterday's practice, takes the first way.
Ahmad ibn Hanbal's great book takes the second. Today, the book, and why the shelving matters.

teach.b: Its name is the Musnad. A musnad report has its chain of narrators attached, leaning back link by link to the Prophet. A book called a Musnad is arranged by Companion, the person who heard the Prophet.
Open it and you find the reports of Abu Bakr together, then those of 'Umar, and on through the Companions, men and women, each with a section of their own.
A reader hunting one topic has to search; a reader who wants one Companion's voice finds it all in one place. It is vast.
His biographers say he gathered it across a lifetime, choosing it from the far larger body of reports he had heard, and meant it as a reference when people disagreed over a sunnah.
His son 'Abd Allah is reported to have heard it from him and passed it on, adding reports of his own.

teach.h: STRONG AND WEAKER, SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: Because Ahmad included reports he judged usable, not only the strongest, strong and weaker reports sit side by side. Later scholars graded them one by one, and some modern editions print a grade beside each.
So the Musnad isn't a law book, or a book of only the strongest hadith.

It's a storehouse. Some of its reports appear in other collections too. Here's one, told by the Companion Anas ibn Malik: none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.
It's in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, and in the Musnad it sits on the shelf of the one who told it.

how: Students of hadith consult Ahmad ibn Hanbal's Musnad by looking up the Companion who narrated a report, and modern printed editions often add scholars' grades beside its reports.

o: Ahmad's book of law, arranged by topic like a code
a collection of only the strongest, sound reports
Ahmad's hadith collection, arranged by Companion

p: Ahmad's son, who passed the book on
love for your brother what you love

s: the Musnad is arranged by subject
it's arranged by the Companion who told each report: Abu Bakr's together, then 'Umar's, and on.
the Musnad holds only the strongest reports
strong and weaker reports sit side by side; later scholars graded them one by one.
a report in the Musnad can also appear in Bukhari and Muslim
the hadith of Anas, love for your brother what you love for yourself, is in all three.

games.q: you're gathering a vast collection of reports from the Prophet. how do you shelve it?
o: by the Companion who told each report.
by how long each report is.
games.why: Ahmad shelved it by Companion. that's what makes it a musnad: finding a topic takes hunting, but each Companion's voice sits in one place.

practice: Read Anas's hadith again, slowly: none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.

Let the word brother sit, with the question of who it covers, then pick one good thing you want for yourself today, rest, good news, a kind word, and name one person you could want that same thing for.
Hold their name for a few breaths, and if you pray, you can ask for it for them.

wordCard.voice: The Musnad. Ahmad ibn Hanbal's collection of hadith, arranged not by topic but by the Companion who told each report. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a report with its chain attached, and a hadith book arranged by Companion.

carryVoice: Your line: a vast collection. Every report kept on the shelf of the one who told it. I'll be here tomorrow.
